1.pericope_label: For, behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, doth take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread, and the whole stay of water, the mighty man, and the man of war, the judge, and the prophet, and the prudent, and the ancient
debates: What the stay and the staff are: Clarke and Calvin take the masculine and feminine pair as every kind of support without limiting it to persons, while Ellicott suspects the explanation as bread and water is a marginal gloss and reads the phrase of the pillars of the state, the great women as well as the great men.

Whether the prudent is a good word or a bad one: Ellicott takes it as diviners who had abused a real gift, Henry allows either sense, and Calvin argues for the good sense while refusing to quarrel with those who read it of magical arts.
outliers: Calvin distinguishes two ways God removes the staff of bread, by withholding food and by withdrawing its power to nourish, so that the belly may be filled and hunger remain.
Henry reports but declines the application of the verse to the decay of the Jewish nation after the crucifixion, preferring to read it as a warning to all nations.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the military opening of the list by the growth of Judah into a military state under Uzziah and Jotham.
themes: A state stripped of its leaders

3.pericope_label: The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator. And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them. And the people shall be oppressed, every one by another, and every one by his neighbour
debates: Who the children given as princes are: Ellicott and Clarke look for actual boy kings and name candidates, while Calvin refuses to limit the word to age and reads it of rulers childish in mind and conduct.
What the cunning artificer is: Ellicott argues for masters in arts, ranking with engineers or artists, but reports that some critics take the word as magician.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch observe that the king is deliberately left unnamed because he had sunk to the shadow of a king, led about by the aristocratic party around him.
Calvin turns the passage into a defence of civil government, arguing that those who would banish the use of the sword and all magistracy are enemies of the public safety.
Ellicott compares the portrait of anarchy with a famous ancient account of a corrupted democracy and says it might have been drawn from his own century.
themes: Government as a gift of God

6.pericope_label: And when a man shall take hold of his brother of the house of his father, saying, Thou hast clothing, be thou our ruler ... In that day shall he swear, saying, I will not be an healer; for in my house is neither bread nor clothing: make me not a ruler of the people. For Jerusalem is ruined, and Judah is fallen
debates: What the gesture of taking hold means: Clarke reads it as humble supplication, on the analogy of other places where a skirt is grasped in entreaty, while Calvin takes the verb as laying hands on a man and has the people seizing a ruler with disorder and violence.

Whether the text reads eyes or cloud in the last clause: Clarke suspects the received word is corrupt and would read cloud, following one ancient version, but allows that either gives a very good sense, and Ellicott keeps eyes as deliberate anthropomorphism.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch trace the sequence despotism, mob-rule, anarchy, and read the coat as the last qualification left for office.
Clarke suspects a word meaning chief or head has dropped out of the text, since brother of his father’s house is little better than a tautology.
Clarke explains the plea of having neither bread nor clothing by the Eastern expectation that a ruler keep great stores for gifts and hospitality, not by simple poverty.

9.pericope_label: The shew of their countenance doth witness against them; and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not. Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves. Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him: for they shall eat the fruit of their doings
debates: What the rare word for their countenance means: Gill reports a derivation giving the knowledge of their faces, Keil and Delitzsch refuse a proposal that would make it mean impudence outright, and Clarke follows a rendering that gives steadfastness.

How the word to the righteous should be read: Clarke calls the text very dubious and canvasses conjectural readings, Calvin argues that to say here means to hold as settled rather than to address anyone, and Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering praise the righteous.
outliers: Clarke compares faces that advertise their own wickedness to the sonorous rings in the tail of the rattlesnake, which announce the presence of the destroyer.
Ellicott leaves undecided whether the likeness to Sodom is general, in luxury and profligacy, or more definite and horrible.

Calvin reads the promise as an answer to the temptation that public calamities spare neither good nor bad, and takes the contrasted words as prosperous and wretched conditions rather than as virtue and wickedness.
themes: No shame left to restrain them

11.pericope_label: Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him. As for my people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths
debates: What the word rendered children means: Keil and Delitzsch reject both maltreaters and suckling and settle on boys at play, while Clarke offers a reading that removes the children and the women altogether, giving grape-gatherers and usurers.

Who the misleaders are: Calvin weighs a rendering that would make them flatterers calling the people happy, and though he grants that false prophets did flatter, he prefers to keep the rulers themselves as the cause of the ruin.
outliers: Calvin states the difficulty the passage answers, that a calamity striking good and bad alike tempts men to think the world governed by blind chance.
Calvin says nothing worse can befall us than to be hardened against chastisement and not perceive who is chastising.
Ellicott identifies the child ruler with Ahaz and traces the corruption downwards from the throne through princes, priests and judges.

13.pericope_label: The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people. The LORD will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof: for ye have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses. What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor?
debates: Whom the Lord stands up to judge: Keil and Delitzsch read the nations and take the scene as the judgment of the world, Clarke notes that the old Greek version reads his people, and Gill refers the whole pleading to the rejection of the Son.

What the verb rendered eaten up means: Calvin argues that its usual sense of burning does not suit men who make a profit of what they consume, and would take it of eating down the produce as cattle eat down grass.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish standing up, sitting down and standing as three distinct descriptions of God rising from his throne, taking the judgment-seat, and coming forward as accuser.
Keil and Delitzsch argue that the clause the divine speech answers is suppressed by God himself rather than by the prophet, since his very appearance was proof of the trust he had given.
Calvin says the palace of princes ought to resemble a sanctuary, so that filling it with the spoil of the poor is the grossest sacrilege.
themes: Rulers who devoured what they guarded
The poor with no protector left

16.pericope_label: Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet: Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion
debates: What the phrase rendered wanton eyes means: Clarke argues at length that it describes eyes falsely set off with paint and gathers evidence for the custom, while Calvin reports the same derivation and rejects it, holding that the prophet is describing affected motions of the body rather than ornaments.

What the tinkling is: Ellicott is confident it means small silver bells fastened at the ankles, a custom he says survives, while Calvin cannot decide between ornaments that made a noise and a measured step imitating dancing women.
Whether the scab is disease or violence: Ellicott divides the threat between illness bred by captivity and the stripping of captives by invaders, and Clarke dwells on the second alone.
outliers: Henry defends the prophet for noticing dress at all, saying God’s law takes cognizance even of that.
Calvin explains that the indictment starts from pride rather than clothing because beginning with the signs would have invited the answer that the mind was still pure.
Calvin refuses to identify the individual ornaments, since the best Hebrew scholars cannot distinguish their forms with certainty.
themes: Pride showing itself in the walk

18.pericope_label: In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon, the chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers, the bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs ... the glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails
debates: What the nose jewels were: Clarke insists on rings hanging from bored nostrils and calls the rival account ridiculous, while Wesley describes them as fastened to the head and hanging down the forehead.
What the crisping pins were: Ellicott makes them small embroidered purses attached to the girdle, Wesley pins of gold or silver used to curl the hair.

What the glasses were: Wesley and Ellicott read polished metal mirrors, while Gill reports an authority who takes the word for garments so thin that the flesh shows through, the sense the old Greek version adopted.
outliers: Wesley declines the whole lexical problem, saying it is of no concern to understand the differences between these ornaments exactly.
Clarke reports that the Arabic dictionaries, printed and in manuscript, yielded nothing at all for one of the words, so no help was to be had from that language.
Ellicott connects the crescent ornaments with those hung on the camels of the Midianite kings and suggests they were once tied to the worship of Ashtaroth and are now kept against the evil eye.

24.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty. Thy men shall fall by the sword, and thy mighty in the war. And her gates shall lament and mourn; and she being desolate shall sit upon the ground
debates: What the burning is: Ellicott takes it for a brand stamped on the flesh to mark a slave, while Calvin and Wesley read it as sunburn on women who had guarded against the sun with the utmost care.

When the desolation was fulfilled: Gill refers the falling by the sword to the Romans and Keil and Delitzsch compare Roman medals struck after the city fell, but Clarke objects that the passage relates in its first and nearer view to the destruction under Nebuchadnezzar.
outliers: Clarke argues that the last clause is textually damaged, the word for burning being without example, and proposes a conjectural restoration to fill a gap he thinks three or four words long.
Calvin explains the change of address by saying it would be improper to assign more than one husband to one woman, so the words must be spoken to the city.
Clarke describes a coin from his own collection showing the conquered province as a woman seated on the ground beneath a palm tree.
themes: A city stripped and seated in the dust
